paper.title: Division by invariant integers using multiplication
paper.venue: ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI) 1994; SIGPLAN Notices 29(6), 61-72

program.how: written for ounce-core from the paper's CHOOSE_MULTIPLIER (Figure 6.2), its unsigned division sequences (Figures 4.1 and 4.2, N = 32) and the divisibility test of Section 9; the quotient is computed with a multiply-high, shifts and adds only and compared with the CPU's own division; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: the constants the paper states in its worked examples are produced: d = 10 gives m = (2^34+1)/5 = 3435973837, post-shift 3, l = 4; d = 7 gives m = (2^35+3)/7 which exceeds 2^32; d = 14 gives pre-shift 1, m = (2^34+5)/7, post-shift 2; d = 641 has final shift zero (the text's example of the rare case); CHOOSE_MULTIPLIER(3, 31) gives post-shift 0 and m = (2^32+2)/3; for divisibility by 100, the inverse of 25 mod 2^32 is (19*2^32+1)/25 = 3264175145 and qmax = (2^31-48)/25 = 85899344

the multiply-and-shift sequences of Figure 4.2 return floor(n/d) exactly, compared with the CPU division, for 65598 divisors (every d = 1..65536 plus 62 further divisors up to 2^31-1) with 100 dividends each (6559800 quotients, 0 wrong)

the Section 9 divisibility test for signed d = 100 (q0 = MULL(dinv, i) is a multiple of 4 inside [-qmax, qmax]) agrees with i mod 100 = 0 on 4286632 32-bit values (every 1021st value plus all values within 20000 of -2^31, 0 and 2^31-1), 0 wrong

expected_values_source.what: the worked-example constants and the divisibility-by-100 example printed in the paper (Sections 4, 5, 9 and Figure 6.2), copied as numbers; the reference quotients come from the CPU's integer division
expected_values_source.note: the text was extracted from the authors' PDF; the paper gives its example constants as expressions such as (2^34+1)/5, which the program compares exactly. The division results are not published numbers, they are checked against the arithmetic of the machine the program runs on, ounce-core's UDIV on the aarch64 side and the host CPU in the native comparison.

negative_control: built with -DGM_ADD=0 (the 2^(N+l-prec) term is left out of m_high in CHOOSE_MULTIPLIER, so the multiplier is rounded down), the example constants no longer match (d = 10 gives post-shift 4, d = 641 gives final shift 10), 3473111 of 6559800 quotients are wrong and the program exits 1
not_checked: the signed and floor-division sequences (Figures 5.2, 6.1), the double-word divisions of Section 8 and the floating-point variant of Section 7
divisors above 2^31 and word sizes other than 32 bits (the 64-bit constants such as d = 274177 are not computed)

exhaustive checking over all 2^32 dividends: about 100 dividends per divisor are used, concentrated near multiples of d and the ends of the range, so the check is evidence, not a proof (the paper proves it as Theorem 4.2)
the paper's timing tables (Tables 1.1 and 11.2) and the GCC implementation
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about the authors' hardware)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, reproduces the paper's stated example constants and shows the generated multiply-shift code agrees with real division on 6.56 million tested (divisor, dividend) pairs. It does not prove Theorem 4.2 for all inputs.
